stories.headline: Colorado's semiautomatic rifle training requirement takes effect
stories.summary:
Coloradans seeking to purchase rifles and shotguns with detachable magazines or gas-operated pistols must now obtain an eligibility card from a sheriff's office and complete a state-approved training course before buying such firearms. Senate Bill 3, signed into law in 2025, went into full effect Saturday after a delayed implementation period allowed time to establish rules, train instructors, and expand background check capacity.

Colorado Parks and Wildlife developed a required curriculum, the Department of Revenue published a list of roughly 1,000 affected firearms, and the Colorado Bureau of Investigation cross-trained 20 staffers to handle increased background check volume. More than 1,000 instructors across the state registered to offer the mandatory training.

Opponents have filed a lawsuit challenging the law on Second Amendment grounds, and backers said they are considering seeking a preliminary injunction. The County Sheriffs of Colorado said its members will carry out their responsibilities under the law but called it an unfunded mandate on local governments.

Supporters, including national gun-safety organization Everytown for Gun Safety, called the rollout a landmark that could serve as a model for other states. Gov. Jared Polis defended the law as protecting both Second Amendment rights and public safety.

stories.headline: Adams County man sentenced to life in prison for domestic violence abduction and murder of Westminster woman
stories.summary:
Jesse Gladney, 38, was sentenced Friday to life in prison without the possibility of parole after an Adams County jury convicted him of first-degree murder on July 24. The sentence is mandatory under Colorado law for first-degree murder convictions.

Witnesses saw Gladney force 36-year-old Valarie Garcia into an SUV in the parking lot of a Super 8 motel at 12055 N. Melody Drive in Westminster on June 8, 2024. According to investigators, Gladney had called someone for a ride, then retrieved Garcia from the building, argued with her and threatened her before shooting her in the chest inside the vehicle.

Garcia was transported to Platte Valley Medical Center in Brighton, where she later died. District Attorney Brian Mason called the killing 'a brutal and senseless killing' and said he was glad the case delivered 'some amount of justice for Valarie Garcia.'

The case highlights the lethality of domestic violence incidents in the Denver metro area. An attorney for Gladney could not be reached for comment.

stories.headline: Broncos stadium president acknowledges frustration with Burnham Yard process, warns 2031 opening at risk
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos president Damani Leech said Saturday that the team's target of opening a new retractable-roof stadium at Burnham Yard in 2031 remains possible but is contingent on accelerating several stalled community and governmental processes. Speaking at the team's new Broncos Park headquarters during training camp, Leech said construction must begin by late spring or early summer of 2027 to meet the 2031 deadline, given a projected three-and-a-half to four-year build time.

Leech expressed frustration that engagement with community groups involved in the Community Benefits Agreement process has largely been conducted at a staff level rather than directly with community members. The 16-organization Burnham Yard Community Action coalition, formed in May, responded that the Broncos ownership group has not yet answered detailed questions the coalition submitted twice and had not responded to a meeting proposal made four weeks prior.

Relocation of Denver Water facilities occupying roughly 20 acres of the Burnham Yard site remains another unresolved complication. Leech said he holds weekly meetings with Denver Water and called its relocation 'a critical component' of the overall deal.

The team also announced Friday that architecture firm Manica has been selected as lead design architect for the new stadium, with Denver-based Tryba Architects named master plan architect for the broader Burnham Yard development. A small area plan between the Broncos and the city could potentially come before the City Council in January, a source told The Denver Post.

stories.headline: Broncos training camp Day 2: Sam Ehlinger takes second-team QB reps over Jarrett Stidham
stories.summary:
Sam Ehlinger took all second-team quarterback reps during Saturday's practice at Broncos Park, the second full day of Denver's 2026 training camp, with Jarrett Stidham running the third-team offense for the first time since Ehlinger joined the organization in March 2025. The shift signals a potential competition for the backup job behind starter Bo Nix, though head coach Sean Payton downplayed the significance of the rep change.

'There was nothing remarkable, or anything we discussed in meeting,' Payton said. Ehlinger re-signed with Denver in March on a one-year, $2 million deal, while Stidham carries an $8 million cap hit in the final year of a two-year, $12 million contract.

Ehlinger largely outperformed Stidham by eye test during the offseason program and had a strong start to camp. Payton has repeatedly said he views Stidham as a starter-caliber NFL quarterback, and Stidham retains goodwill within the organization despite a shaky outing in January's AFC Championship loss to New England.

Also notable from Day 2: wide receiver Marvin Mims Jr. and the first-team offense drew attention for big plays, while tight end Caleb Lohner remained sidelined with a lower-body injury and outside linebacker Drew Sanders continued to miss practice for undisclosed reasons.

stories.headline: NCAA eligibility injunction could expand CU Buffs rosters ahead of football preseason
stories.summary:
A federal judge in Denver granted an injunction Friday allowing all college athletes from the 2022 graduating class — those who used four years of eligibility through the 2025-26 academic year — an additional year of eligibility. The ruling by U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney comes on top of an earlier NCAA rule expanding all athletes to five years of eligibility.

The timing creates immediate complications for Colorado Buffaloes athletic programs. CU football opens its fourth preseason under head coach Deion Sanders on Sunday in Colorado Springs; the team carried 95 players in the spring, leaving room to add returning seniors before the Sept. 3 season opener at Georgia Tech.

For CU men's basketball coach Tad Boyle, the roster is already at the 15-player limit, meaning he would need to cut players to accommodate any returners. Women's basketball coach JR Payne has one open roster spot and is monitoring the status of former All-Big 12 honoree Jade Masogayo, who fits the new eligibility parameters.

Boyle said the ruling underscores the ongoing instability in college athletics. 'I think the only way we get to a hard set of rules with teeth in the transfer area is if we have collective bargaining,' he said.

stories.headline: Colorado marks 150th birthday with statewide celebrations, downtown Denver festival
stories.summary:
Coloradans gathered across the state Saturday to celebrate the 150th anniversary of Colorado's statehood, with the largest events centered in downtown Denver near the History Colorado Center, Central Library, and Denver Art Museum. History Colorado hosted a community festival featuring a free pancake breakfast, food trucks, art installations, and live music, including performances of John Denver's 'Rocky Mountain High' and 'Take Me Home, Country Roads' by Boulder-born musician Isaac Slade on a guitar that belonged to Denver himself.

Gov. Jared Polis, dressed in a velvet cowboy outfit in Colorado colors, gave remarks at the festival and cut a birthday cake on the steps of the State Capitol. Polis called John Denver his favorite artist and said his first concert was a Denver show at Red Rocks.

History Colorado president and CEO Dawn DiPrince said the event had been in planning for three years, with a goal of fostering community connection. 'These in many ways can feel like polarizing times, and we wanted to do the opposite of that,' DiPrince said.

Attendees at the History Colorado Center received free admission to several exhibits dedicated to Colorado's path to statehood. Residents from across the metro, including transplants from California, Louisiana, and beyond, said the milestone reinforced their pride in calling Colorado home.

stories.headline: RTD's East Colfax bus rapid transit project protected from service cuts by $150 million federal grant
stories.summary:
Route 15 along East Colfax Avenue — Denver's busiest bus corridor and the future home of a new bus rapid transit line — is effectively shielded from RTD's planned 2027 service cuts because of a $150 million Federal Transit Administration grant that the agency would have to repay if it eliminated service on the route within a set timeframe. RTD's board voted last week to pursue $20 million in bus and light-rail cuts systemwide to address an estimated $200 million budget shortfall.

RTD spokesperson Pauline Haberman said cutting route 15 is 'highly unlikely,' citing the federal grant obligations and the fact that the East Colfax corridor is the agency's highest-ridership bus line. Denver Department of Transportation and Infrastructure project director Jon Stewart said the grant effectively acts as both a constraint and an incentive for RTD.

Construction on the East Colfax BRT corridor between Broadway and Colorado Boulevard is more than halfway complete and running ahead of schedule. Dedicated BRT lanes in that stretch are expected to open to regular route 15 service this fall, though the new BRT vehicles will not be available until the full project is completed at the end of 2027.

Construction crews are now ramping up work along the Aurora portion of the corridor. City officials said their biggest challenge has been helping businesses navigate reduced customer traffic during the construction period.

stories.headline: Colorado drought deepens: record-low streamflows, threatened hydropower, fishing closures spread statewide
stories.summary:
More than half of Colorado is now classified in extreme or exceptional drought — the two most severe categories — according to the latest U.S. Drought Monitor data, with conditions barely changed from the prior week despite some monsoon rainfall in July. State engineer Jason Ullmann told water managers last month that streamflow gauges across Colorado are at or near record lows, comparing the state to the barren landscape of Mordor.

The 2026 water year, which began in October, is the warmest on record and the fourth-driest, according to the Colorado Department of Natural Resources. A winter snowpack that reached only 58 percent of normal has left reservoirs severely depleted — some now resemble rivers — and boat ramps across the state no longer reach the water's surface.

Farmers across the state have fallowed unprecedented shares of cropland, and rising water temperatures in shrunken rivers are causing fish to suffocate, prompting record fishing restrictions. At least two dams are facing declining reservoir levels that now threaten hydropower production.

Water officials say the monsoon season can reduce demand but will not replenish storage to normal levels. 'The whole state is feeling the pain and the strain of this year's drought,' said Emily Adrid of the Colorado Water Conservation Board.

stories.headline: No arrests made after illegal street takeover at Denver's Broadway and Mississippi intersection
stories.summary:
Denver police responded to an illegal street takeover near midnight Friday at the intersection of Broadway and Mississippi Avenue but made no arrests and issued no citations. Video recorded by residents and shared on social media showed cars performing donuts, large crowds cheering, fireworks being set off in the intersection, and a fire started in the roadway.

Denver Police Department spokesperson Doug Schepman said officers began arriving at approximately 12:16 a.m. and cleared the area using lights and sirens. One resident told Denver7 the event lasted roughly 30 minutes before police arrived, and that the fireworks and fire were 'incredibly loud and anxiety-inducing.'

Schepman said the delayed response time was likely due to higher-priority calls for service in the district. He described the reckless driving and blocked intersection as 'incredibly dangerous and concerning' and noted that potential penalties for street racing include jail time, court costs, and vehicle seizure under Denver's Public Nuisance Abatement ordinance.

Denver police have conducted street racing suppression operations for several years. So far in 2026, DPD has made at least 59 arrests, impounded 44 vehicles, and issued 289 citations related to street racing and speed exhibition.

stories.headline: ICE-detained Ecuadorian woman arrested at Denver International Airport released from Aurora detention center
stories.summary:
An Ecuadorian woman whose arrest by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at Denver International Airport went viral last week was released from federal custody Thursday afternoon, according to her attorney. The woman had been held at the immigration detention facility in Aurora following her arrest at DIA.

The arrest drew widespread attention after video of the incident circulated on social media, prompting public debate about immigration enforcement practices at Denver's airport. Details of the circumstances leading to her release were not immediately disclosed.

The incident adds to ongoing tensions between federal immigration authorities and Denver-area officials over enforcement practices. ICE operations in the Denver metro have generated significant controversy in recent months.

stories.headline: West Metro firefighter in critical condition after 50-foot fall during training exercise near Morrison
stories.summary:
A West Metro Fire Rescue firefighter is in critical but stable condition after falling approximately 50 feet during a training exercise near Morrison on Wednesday, according to CPR News. The firefighter was taken to a hospital following the incident.

Details about the specific nature of the training exercise and the exact location near Morrison were not immediately available. West Metro Fire Rescue serves communities including Lakewood, Wheat Ridge, and unincorporated Jefferson County.

The incident comes during a period of heightened attention to firefighter safety in Colorado following the deaths of multiple firefighters in a wildfire burnover in Mesa County last month. The condition of the injured firefighter was described as critical but stable as of Thursday.

stories.headline: Wildfire near Pagosa Springs grows to 440 acres, forces mandatory evacuations of 373 homes
stories.summary:
A wildfire burning near Pagosa Springs in southwestern Colorado has grown to 440 acres and prompted mandatory evacuation orders for 373 homes, according to fire officials. The blaze is the latest in a series of wildfires burning across the state amid severe drought conditions.

The fire's location near Pagosa Springs in Archuleta County threatens a residential area in the San Juan Mountains region. Firefighting resources have been stretched thin across Colorado this summer as multiple large fires burn simultaneously.

Mandatory evacuations require residents in the affected areas to leave immediately, with evacuation centers established for displaced residents. Containment information was not immediately available.

The fire adds to the toll of a wildfire season fueled by record drought, record heat, and below-normal snowpack. State officials have described this summer as among the most challenging in recent memory for fire and water resource management.

topStory.headline: Migrants Return to Morocco From Spain's Ceuta After Finding Hunger, Closed Shops and Hostility
topStory.summary:
Hundreds of migrants who breached the heavily fortified border into Spain's African enclave of Ceuta this week have begun returning to Morocco, their hopes of reaching mainland Europe dashed within days. Those heading back cited an inability to find food, a lack of any viable path forward to the Spanish mainland, and reports of hostility from some residents of the enclave's predominantly Moroccan neighborhood of El Principe.

Many of the returnees said they had been drawn to attempt the crossing after viral social-media videos showed thousands of people breaching the border simultaneously. Brahim, a bakery worker from the Moroccan city of Fez who left his job to make the crossing, told Reuters he survived three days on water alone and was shocked by food prices on the Spanish side. "We came to make progress, not to be fooled," he said. "I thought I'd build a better future there. But I was surprised in Ceuta." Another returnee described Ceuta as "like a prison — nothing to do there. Everything was closed."

Some migrants reported being physically driven out of the El Principe neighborhood, though Reuters was unable to independently verify those accounts. Spain's Interior Ministry confirmed that two people sustained minor injuries in separate knife attacks and that one assailant had been arrested, while stating that no deaths from knife attacks had been recorded in Ceuta since Thursday. Moroccan waiter Yassine Ichou said he was hit and chased away from El Principe, alleging that a coordinated effort involving shop closures was used to pressure migrants into leaving voluntarily.

In Fnideq, the Moroccan border city directly opposite Ceuta, streets that had teemed with thousands of would-be crossers on Thursday were reported nearly empty by Saturday, with young men walking or waiting for taxis to depart the area. Across the border, Ceuta began showing signs of returning to normalcy, with some cafes reopening even as most shops remained shuttered and police maintained a visible presence on the streets. The episode underscores the persistent pressure on Spain's two African enclaves, Ceuta and Melilla, which serve as the only land borders between Africa and the European Union and have long been focal points for migration attempts from Morocco and sub-Saharan Africa.

The mass crossing and rapid reversal highlight the volatile dynamics at Spain's southern frontier, where the flow of migrants is heavily influenced by both Moroccan border enforcement and shifting conditions on the ground in the enclaves themselves. Spanish and Moroccan authorities have not publicly detailed coordinated steps taken in response to this week's events, and it remains unclear what formal measures either government plans to implement to prevent a recurrence. The incident is expected to renew political debate within Spain and the broader European Union over border management and migrant policy at the EU's external frontiers.
